lesson.title: The Pen Behind the Declaration: Thomas Jefferson
lesson.summary: Thomas Jefferson, the primary author of the Declaration of Independence, was a Virginia planter and Enlightenment thinker whose ideals of liberty stood in stark contrast to his lifelong ownership of enslaved people.
lesson.body:
Thomas Jefferson was born on April 13, 1743, at Shadwell, his family's plantation in the Virginia Piedmont. He trained as a lawyer, studied at the College of William and Mary, and developed a wide ranging intellectual life that touched architecture, science, and philosophy alongside politics and law. By his early thirties he had already built a reputation in Virginia as a clear and forceful writer, which is why the Second Continental Congress turned to him in June 1776 to draft the document explaining the colonies' break from Britain.

Jefferson was only thirty three years old when he wrote the Declaration of Independence, working mostly alone in rented rooms in Philadelphia before submitting his draft to the committee and then the full Congress for revision. The document's soaring language about natural rights and government by consent reflected Jefferson's deep reading in Enlightenment philosophy, particularly the ideas of John Locke, and it established Jefferson as one of the intellectual architects of the American cause even before he held major national office.

Jefferson's career extended far beyond 1776. He served as governor of Virginia during the difficult later years of the Revolutionary War, then represented the new United States as minister to France in the 1780s, where he observed the early stages of the French Revolution and corresponded with Lafayette and other French reformers. Under President Washington he served as the first Secretary of State, and he later served one term as the second Vice President under John Adams before being elected the third President of the United States in 1800, in an election so contested it had to be settled in the House of Representatives.

As president, Jefferson's most consequential act was the Louisiana Purchase of 1803, which bought a vast territory from France and roughly doubled the size of the United States, opening the way for westward expansion for generations to come and prompting the expedition of Meriwether Lewis and William Clark to explore it. Later in life he designed his own home at Monticello and founded the University of Virginia, an achievement he considered among his greatest, and he continued to correspond widely on politics and philosophy until his final years.

Jefferson's legacy carries a painful contradiction that historians continue to grapple with. The man who wrote that all men are created equal owned several hundred enslaved people over the course of his life, including at Monticello, and he fathered children with an enslaved woman, Sally Hemings, whom he did not free during her lifetime. Understanding Jefferson honestly means holding both truths together: he gave the Revolution its most powerful statement of human equality, and he personally denied that equality to the people he held in bondage. Jefferson died on July 4, 1826, exactly fifty years after the Declaration's adoption, on the very same day as John Adams.
